semantics: The result is the number of distinct values of the analysis variable on the records of the cell.
A missing value is not counted. For text, the empty text is a missing value.
A cell without records gives 0, not a missing result.
Text values are compared exactly, as they are stored. Case and blanks count.
count.subjects.takes: the values of the analysis variable on the records of one cell
count.subjects.title: Count of subjects

semantics: A pattern is text with exactly one mask. A mask is a run of the capital letter X, with or without one decimal point inside it and X on both sides of the point: "XX", "XX.X". The text before and after the mask is kept as it is: "(N=XX)" has "(N=" before and ")" after. A pattern with no mask or with two is refused.
The number is rounded by display.round.half_away_from_zero to as many decimals as the mask has X after its point, and to a whole number when the mask has no point.

A mask with a decimal point: the rounded number, without its sign, is padded with blanks on the left to the length of the mask. 9.52 under "( XX.X)" is "( 9.5)". A number that is longer than the mask is not cut.
A mask without a decimal point: the rounded number is not padded. 8 under "XXX" is "8".
A negative number has its minus sign before the padding: -3.3 under "XX.X" is "- 3.3". A number that rounds to zero has no sign.
A missing number gives a missing result.
For a mock shell the mask itself stands in place of the number, in lower case: "( xx.x)". No number is needed.
With the option rounding set to half_even, the number is rounded by display.round.half_even in place of the rule of statement 2. Statements 3 to 7 hold as they stand.
display.pattern.takes: one number and a pattern, such as "( XX.X)"
display.pattern.title: A number shown by a result pattern

semantics: The number is first written as the shortest decimal that reads back as the same double. That decimal is what is rounded, not the binary value behind it. 2.675 is rounded as 2.675, although the nearest double is a little below it.
The decimal is rounded to the asked count of decimals. A decimal exactly halfway between two results goes to the one farther from zero.
The result is text with exactly that count of decimals, and without a decimal point when the count is 0. It has no exponent and no thousands separator.
A result that is zero has no minus sign.
A missing number gives a missing result. Infinity and not-a-number are refused.
display.round.half_away_from_zero.takes: one number and the count of decimals to show, 0 to 15
display.round.half_away_from_zero.title: Round half away from zero

semantics: The number is first written as the shortest decimal that reads back as the same double, as in display.round.half_away_from_zero. That decimal is what is rounded, not the binary value behind it.

The decimal is rounded to the asked count of decimals. A decimal exactly halfway between two results goes to the one whose last digit is even: 0.125 gives 0.12, 0.135 gives 0.14, 2.5 gives 2 and 3.5 gives 4.
A decimal that is not exactly halfway goes to the nearer result, as in display.round.half_away_from_zero: the two rules differ at a half only.
The result is text with exactly that count of decimals, and without a decimal point when the count is 0. It has no exponent and no thousands separator.
A result that is zero has no minus sign.
A missing number gives a missing result. Infinity and not-a-number are refused.
display.round.half_even.takes: one number and the count of decimals to show, 0 to 15
display.round.half_even.title: Round half to even

semantics: The result is 100 times the numerator divided by the denominator.
The numerator is the result of the operation that the analysis references with the role NUMERATOR, in the same cell.

The denominator is the result of the operation that the analysis references with the role DENOMINATOR, in the analysis named there. It is the one result of that analysis whose groups are all groups of the cell. No such result, or more than one, is an error.
When the denominator is 0 or missing, the result is missing. It is never infinite.
When the numerator is missing, the result is missing.
The result is not rounded and not capped at 100.
percent.subjects.takes: two results that the analysis references, a numerator and a denominator
percent.subjects.title: Percent of subjects, with a referenced denominator

semantics: The values are the non-missing values of the analysis variable on the records of the cell.
n: the number of values. A cell without values gives 0.
mean: the sum of the values divided by n. Missing when n is 0.
sd: the square root of the sum of squared differences from the mean, divided by the denominator of the option sd_denominator. Missing when n is less than 2.
min and max: the smallest and the largest value. Missing when n is 0.
median, q1 and q3: the quantile at p = 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 of the sorted values x[1] <= ... <= x[n], by the definition of the option quantile_definition. Missing when n is 0.

quantile_definition sas5 (SAS QNTLDEF=5, the default of SAS; R type 2): write n * p = j + g with j an integer and 0 <= g < 1. The quantile is x[j + 1] when g > 0, and (x[j] + x[j + 1]) / 2 when g = 0. For the three values of p here, g = 0 exactly when n * 4 * p is divisible by 4, so no tolerance is involved.

quantile_definition r7 (R type 7, the default of R and of NumPy): write (n - 1) * p = j + g with j an integer and 0 <= g < 1. The quantile is x[j + 1] + g * (x[j + 2] - x[j + 1]), and x[j + 1] when g = 0.
The median is the same number under both definitions.

sd: 0 when the smallest and the largest value are equal. This is decided by comparing the values, not by the arithmetic of statement 4, which can leave a rounding error of the mean (three values of 0.1).
summary.continuous.takes: the values of the analysis variable on the records of one cell
summary.continuous.title: Summary of a continuous variable

semantics: Missing values are left out. A group without values is left out.
With k groups and N values in all, the result is missing when k is less than 2 or N - k is less than 1.

SSB is the sum over the groups of n[i] * (mean[i] - grand mean)^2, and SSW the sum over all values of (value - mean of its group)^2. The statistic is F = (SSB / (k - 1)) / (SSW / (N - k)). The variances of the groups are taken as equal: this is not the Welch test.
p_value: the probability that an F variable with k - 1 and N - k degrees of freedom is at least F.

When no group holds two different values, SSW is 0 and F is not computed: the result is 0 if the groups do not all hold the same value, and missing if they do. This case is decided by comparing the values, not by a sum that rounding could leave just above 0.
test.anova.oneway.takes: the values of the analysis variable in each of k groups
test.anova.oneway.title: One-way analysis of variance

semantics: Rows and columns whose total is 0 are left out.
With fewer than 2 rows or fewer than 2 columns left, the result is missing.
The expected count of a cell is its row total times its column total, divided by the total N. The statistic is the sum over the cells of (count - expected)^2 / expected.
No continuity correction is applied, whatever the size of the table.
p_value: the probability that a chi-square variable with (r - 1) * (c - 1) degrees of freedom is at least the statistic.
Small expected counts change nothing and give no warning.
test.chisq.takes: a table of counts with r rows and c columns
test.chisq.title: Pearson chi-square test

semantics: Rows and columns whose total is 0 are left out.
With fewer than 2 rows or fewer than 2 columns left, the result is missing.
The probability of a table with the row totals R[i], the column totals C[j] and the total N is the product of the R[i]! and the C[j]!, divided by N! and by the product of the factorials of its cells.

p_value: the sum of the probabilities of all tables with the row and column totals of the observed table whose probability is not larger than that of the observed table. The test is two-sided for every size of table.

"Not larger" allows a relative excess of 1e-7, so that tables of the same probability count whatever the rounding. This is the allowance of R's fisher.test for a 2 x 2 table; for a larger table see statement 8.

The sum is over every such table: no sampling and no approximation, for a 2 x 2 table and for a larger one. A table with more than 10,000,000 tables to sum is refused with an error, by both implementations.
A sum above 1 by rounding gives 1.

Implementations. Python sums over every table, for every size. R gives a 2 x 2 table to fisher.test and sums over every table itself for a larger one: there fisher.test allows a wider excess than statement 5 and counts a table that is more probable than the observed one by a relative 2.7e-7 or 3.2e-7, which changes the p-value by several percent.
test.fisher.exact.takes: a table of counts with r rows and c columns
test.fisher.exact.title: Fisher exact test
